summary: Describes provisioning models, auto-discovery, and signaling for provider-provisioned Layer 2 VPNs, where discovery distributes the configuration and signaling then sets up the mesh of pseudowires.

plainLanguage.summary: A layer 2 VPN carries whole Ethernet frames between customer sites, and the provider has to build a mesh of pseudowires to do it. This RFC says how the two ends of each pseudowire name each other, how the provider finds out which ends belong together, and how the signalling protocols carry those names.

questions: what is bgp auto-discovery for vpls
subtitle: How layer 2 VPN endpoints are named, discovered with BGP and connected with LDP or L2TPv3 pseudowires.

tldr.problem: Provider-provisioned layer 2 VPNs come in several kinds, each configured differently, yet the signaling protocols that build their pseudowires need one general way to name the endpoints.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines provisioning models and the structure of the endpoint identifiers each needs, an Attachment Group Identifier plus source and target Attachment Individual Identifiers, shows how BGP carries them in auto-discovery, and how LDP and L2TPv3 encode them.
tldr.outcome: A discovery step finds which endpoints belong together and signaling then sets up the pseudowire mesh automatically, including across autonomous systems. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 6074 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2011. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 4664 for the service models, and on the LDP and L2TP extensions in RFC 4447 and RFC 4667 for the signalling.

sections.title: Why L2VPN Signalling Needs a Common Naming Scheme
sections.content:
RFC 4664 describes several ways of combining pseudowires into provider-provisioned layer 2 VPNs, and each kind of L2VPN has its own provisioning model, meaning its own set of facts that have to be configured and where. Once configured, a discovery process distributes that information, and once the information has been discovered, the signalling protocol is invoked automatically to set up the pseudowires. The semantics of the endpoint identifiers the signalling protocol uses depend on the provisioning model, so different kinds of L2VPN need different kinds of endpoint identifier.

Either LDP or L2TP version 3 can be used to set up and maintain pseudowires, and any protocol that sets up connections must give each end a way to identify the other. Since each signalling protocol has to support all the kinds of L2VPN and all their provisioning models, it needs a very general way of representing endpoint identifiers, and rules for encoding each kind of identifier into the fields of each protocol. That is what this document specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: Different kinds of layer 2 VPN are configured differently, but the signalling protocols have to work for all of them. The trick is a general way of naming the two ends of a pseudowire.

sections.title: Forwarders, Attachment Circuits and Endpoint Identifiers
sections.content:
A pseudowire can be thought of as a relationship between a pair of Forwarders. In simple Virtual Private Wire Service, a Forwarder binds one pseudowire to one Attachment Circuit, so that frames received on one are sent on the other. In Virtual Private LAN Service, a Forwarder binds a set of pseudowires to a set of attachment circuits, and a MAC address table decides which of them a received frame is sent on. In more complex cases Forwarders bind pseudowires to pseudowires, splicing two together, which is what distributed VPLS and some inter-AS scenarios need.

In simple VPWS, where a Forwarder binds exactly one pseudowire to exactly one attachment circuit, the Forwarder can be identified by its attachment circuit. In simple VPLS, a Forwarder is identified by its PE device and its VPN.

To set up a pseudowire, the signalling protocol must let one end identify the other. LDP calls the quantity that does this an Attachment Identifier, and L2TP calls the same thing a Forwarder Identifier; the two names are used interchangeably here. LDP offers two FEC elements for this. The PWid element carries only one identifier, so it can be used only when both forwarders have the same identifier and it fits in 32 bits. The Generalized ID element carries two identifiers, one for each forwarder, and a signalling message carries a Source Attachment Identifier and a Target Attachment Identifier.

The identifiers are structured further. The source and target identifiers sometimes share a common part, the Attachment Group Identifier, so that each is the concatenation of that group with an Attachment Individual Identifier. The pair is then encoded in three fields: the AGI, the source AII and the target AII. In applications that group sets of pseudowires into layer 2 VPNs, the AGI can be thought of as a VPN identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end of a pseudowire has a name made of two parts: a group part that says which VPN it belongs to, and an individual part that says which circuit inside that VPN.

sections.title: The AGI, SAII and TAII Fields
sections.content:
Every Forwarder in a PE must have an Attachment Identifier, either from configuration or from an algorithm, and the identifier must be unique within that PE router, so that the pair of PE router and identifier is globally unique. The AGI may be thought of as a VPN identifier, or as some attribute shared by all the attachment circuits that are allowed to be connected. A set of attachment circuits at a single PE can also be considered a pool.

An LSP for one direction of a pseudowire is identified by the pair of PE routers with their identifiers, and the opposite direction by the same pair the other way round. When a message is sent from PE1 to PE2 and PE1 refers to an identifier configured on one of its own attachment circuits, that is the Source Attachment Identifier; when it refers to one configured on PE2, that is the Target Attachment Identifier. An SAI at one end is therefore a TAI at the other, and the other way round.

Three fields are defined: the AGI, the Source Attachment Individual Identifier and the Target Attachment Individual Identifier. If the AGI is not null, the SAI is the AGI together with the SAII, and the TAI is the TAII together with the AGI. If the AGI is null, the SAII and the TAII are the SAI and the TAI on their own. The intention is that the PE receiving a message with a TAI can map that TAI uniquely to one of its attachment circuits or pools. How it does the mapping, and how many bytes of the TAI it uses for it, is a local matter, so as far as signalling is concerned the TAI is just an arbitrary string of bytes, a cookie.
sections.plainLanguage: The three fields put the two names on the wire. The far end just needs to be able to look up its own circuit from what arrives; how it does the lookup is up to it.

sections.title: Individual Point-to-Point Pseudowires
sections.content:
In the simplest application, each Forwarder binds a single pseudowire to a single attachment circuit, and each PE must be provisioned with its attachment circuits and the parameters for each of them.

With double-sided provisioning, each attachment circuit is provisioned with a local name, a remote PE address and a remote name. During signalling the local name is sent as the SAII and the remote name as the TAII, and the AGI is null. For two circuits to be connected, the local name of each must be the remote name of the other. If the two names are the same, the PWid FEC element can be used instead of the Generalized ID element. With L2TP, the local name goes in the Local End ID AVP and the remote name in the Remote End ID AVP, and the AGI AVP is optional.

With single-sided provisioning with discovery, each attachment circuit is provisioned with a local name made of a VPN identifier, signalled as the AGI, and an individual identifier that is unique within that group. Only one of the two circuits needs a remote name, and neither needs the address of the remote PE, but both must have the same VPN identifier. Each PE advertises its pairs of VPN identifier and local individual identifier, and compares them with what the other PEs advertise, so it can discover that it needs to connect. The benefit over double-sided provisioning is that an attachment circuit can move from one PE to another without the remote end being reconfigured, at the cost of a heavier discovery burden, since every circuit name has to be advertised individually.

The LDP signalling follows RFC 4447: one PE sends a Label Mapping message to the other to establish an LSP in one direction, and if that succeeds and there is not yet an LSP in the opposite direction, the other PE sends its own Label Mapping message back. A receiver that finds the attachment circuit is already bound to a different pseudowire, or bound to a different remote attachment circuit than the message names, answers with a Label Release message carrying a status code that says so. The L2TP equivalent is a Call Disconnect Notify message.
sections.plainLanguage: You can configure both ends with each other's names, or configure one end and let the provider work out the rest by advertising the names. Either way, the signalling then sets up the tunnel.

sections.title: VPLS and BGP Auto-Discovery
sections.content:
In VPLS, the attachment circuits are like LAN interfaces attached to virtual switches, called Virtual Switching Instances. Each Forwarder is one such instance, and the service requires a single pseudowire between each pair of instances in the same VPLS.

Each VPLS must have a globally unique identifier, and every instance must be configured with it. Each instance also needs a unique identifier of its own, which can be formed by concatenating the VPLS identifier with an IP address of the PE that holds it, though other numbering schemes are possible. The address is only a source of uniqueness, and does not have to be globally routable.

For BGP-based auto-discovery the address family is an AFI of 25 for L2VPN, the same for all layer 2 VPN schemes, and a SAFI of 65 for an L2VPN service whose pseudowires are set up by these procedures. Each VPLS identifier must be encodable as an 8-byte Route Distinguisher, and each instance identifier as BGP network layer reachability information, formed by prepending that Route Distinguisher to the PE's IP address.

Each VPLS needs a single globally unique identifier, which must be encodable as a BGP Extended Community and must be transitive. The RFC defines two Extended Community subtypes for this, a Two-octet AS Specific one and an IPv4 Address Specific one, so that a provider can allocate an identifier without colliding with another provider. Each instance is also associated with one or more Route Targets, which control the distribution of the information and therefore the shape of the pseudowire mesh. Each PE distributes the information for its own instances through BGP with itself as the next hop, and typically the PEs are clients of a small set of route reflectors. An update missing any of these elements should be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: For a layer 2 LAN service, the provider advertises each of its switches through BGP with a route target that says which LAN it belongs to. Each provider then learns about the other members of the same LAN and builds the pseudowires between them.

sections.title: Colored Pools for Full-Mesh Pseudowires
sections.content:
The colored pools model delivers point-to-point service automatically. Each PE may hold several pools of attachment circuits, each pool tied to a particular VPN, and a PE may hold several pools per VPN, one for each customer device. A pseudowire is created between every pair of pools that have the same color, which for a full mesh of customer circuits means a full mesh of virtual circuits per VPN.

Each pool is configured with a set of attachment circuits, a color that can be thought of as a VPN identifier of some sort, and a relative pool identifier that is unique within the color. The pool identifier together with the color is globally unique, so with n pools of a given color their identifiers can be the numbers 1 to n. A pseudowire is created between every pair of pools with the same color, and each one is bound to one attachment circuit from each of the two pools. If each pool holds the circuits of one customer device, the layer 2 connectivity among the customers is controlled by how the colors are assigned.

Optionally, a particular attachment circuit can be configured with the relative pool identifier of a remote pool, in which case it is bound to a pseudowire only if that pseudowire's remote endpoint is the pool with that identifier, so the same pairs of circuits are always joined. For BGP-based auto-discovery the address family is the same L2VPN AFI with a SAFI for this service. The globally unique identifier of a pool must be encodable as network layer reachability information, and the pool identifier, which is a 4-byte quantity, is appended to the Route Distinguisher to form it. Each pool is also associated with a Route Target, which may be an encoding of the color; for a full mesh all the pools may have the same target.
sections.plainLanguage: Give each group of customer circuits a color, and the provider builds a tunnel between every pair of groups with the same color. The customer only has to say which color each circuit has.

sections.title: Distributed VPLS and Splicing
sections.content:
In distributed VPLS, the VPLS function of a PE is split between two systems. The U-PE sits between the user and the N-PE and does the VSI work, such as MAC address learning and bridging, while a number of U-PEs attach to an N-PE. For each VPLS the U-PE supports, it maintains a pseudowire to each of the other U-PEs in the same VPLS, but the U-PEs keep no signalling connections with each other. Each U-PE has a single signalling connection, to its N-PE.

Each U-PE-to-U-PE pseudowire is therefore made of three pseudowires spliced together: one from the U-PE to the N-PE, one from N-PE to N-PE, and one from N-PE to U-PE. The N-PEs perform the pseudowire switching function that establishes multi-segment pseudowires between the U-PEs.

The RFC works through an example with four U-PEs A, B, C and D in a common VPLS, attached to N-PEs E and F. To connect A to the others there must be two pseudowires from E to F, one from E to B, one from F to C and one from F to D, and the N-PEs splice them so that A reaches B through E, A reaches C through E and F, and A reaches D through E and F. It does not matter which pseudowires are spliced together, as long as the result is one from A to each of B, C and D.
sections.plainLanguage: In a large layer 2 LAN service, the switching is split between a small router at the customer and a bigger one in the middle. The middle routers join the short tunnels together into one long tunnel between the customer routers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points at the documents that hold the security rules for each piece it uses. The signalling protocols are covered by RFC 5036, RFC 4447, RFC 3931 and RFC 4667. The security considerations of BGP-based auto-discovery, including the inter-AS issues, are in RFC 4364, and L2VPNs that use BGP-based auto-discovery may automate the setup of security mechanisms as well, though specifying that is outside the scope of this document and is recommended as future work. The security considerations of the particular kind of layer 2 VPN service are in RFC 4664, RFC 4665 and RFC 4762.

The RFC's own conclusion is that the way endpoint identifiers are mapped into protocol fields does not create any additional security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is added here: the signalling, routing and service documents already say what the security rules are, and mapping the names into protocol fields does not add any risk of its own.
